subject: psychology
title: An initial numerical reference
stem: Explain anchoring bias with reference to one example of a judgement.

steps.text: Anchoring bias occurs when an initial reference has an inappropriate influence on a later judgement, often because adjustment away from it is insufficient. For example, someone estimating how long an unfamiliar journey will take may give excessive weight to an arbitrary duration mentioned before they consider the actual route.

The example requires more than simply using prior information: relevant information can reasonably inform an estimate. The bias is the disproportionate influence of a reference that is not justified by the available evidence. Explaining why the initial duration remains influential distinguishes anchoring from a general statement that people sometimes make inaccurate predictions.

subject: psychology
title: Learning an association between stimuli
stem: Explain classical conditioning with reference to one example of a learned response.

steps.text: Classical conditioning involves learning an association between stimuli. In an illustrative example, an initially neutral sound repeatedly occurs shortly before food that naturally produces salivation. The food is the unconditioned stimulus and salivation to it is the unconditioned response. The sound initially has no such predictive role.

After association, the sound can function as a conditioned stimulus and elicit a conditioned salivary response when food is absent. The learned response need not be identical in every feature to the original response. The explanation concerns a predictive stimulus relationship, rather than a consequence delivered because an individual voluntarily performed a behaviour.

subject: psychology
title: Limited resources during a task
stem: Explain cognitive load theory with reference to one example of learning.

steps.text: Cognitive load theory considers how limited working-memory resources affect learning and the development of organized knowledge. A novice following a complex assembly instruction may need to coordinate unfamiliar components, terminology and actions at once. If demands exceed available resources, the learner may fail to integrate the instructions meaningfully.

For example, placing explanatory labels beside the relevant components can reduce unnecessary searching between separate pages. The goal is to support learning, rather than remove every intellectual challenge. Existing knowledge changes the demands of a task, so the same instruction can impose different loads on a novice and an experienced learner.

subject: psychology
title: A model as an explanatory representation
stem: Explain how one cognitive model can contribute to understanding behaviour, using an example.

steps.text: A cognitive model represents proposed processes and relationships that cannot usually be observed directly. For example, a working-memory model distinguishes processes involved in maintaining verbal and visuospatial information and coordinating attention. This can explain why two concurrent tasks may interfere differently depending on the resources they require.

The model makes predictions that can be compared with behaviour, rather than merely describing an invisible box called thinking. Its components are explanatory constructs, not necessarily separate anatomical containers. A useful example connects a particular prediction to an observable task and recognizes that a successful prediction supports the model without proving that every component is literally represented as drawn.

subject: psychology
title: Testing a favoured explanation
stem: Explain confirmation bias with reference to one example of reasoning.

steps.text: Confirmation bias is a tendency to seek, interpret or remember information in ways that favour an existing belief or hypothesis. For example, a person who believes a particular work routine improves concentration may notice successful sessions using it while overlooking equally successful sessions without it or unsuccessful sessions with it.

The mechanism is selective treatment of evidence, rather than simply possessing an opinion. An accurate explanation identifies what evidence would challenge the belief and how it is neglected or reinterpreted. A conclusion can happen to be correct while still having been reached through biased reasoning, so confirmation bias cannot be identified solely from whether the final belief is false.

subject: psychology
title: Automatic and deliberate processing
stem: Explain dual processing theory with reference to one example of judgement.

steps.text: Dual processing theory distinguishes relatively automatic, rapid processing from more deliberate processing that places greater demands on attention and working memory. An experienced reader may recognize a familiar word with little conscious effort but deliberately inspect an unfamiliar word and its sentence before choosing a meaning.

These are functional distinctions, not a claim that two separate people or anatomical brains make decisions. Automatic processing can be accurate and useful, while deliberate thinking can also support a mistaken interpretation. The example should connect task demands and processing characteristics instead of defining the distinction as fast means wrong and slow means correct.

subject: psychology
title: Consequences and changing behaviour
stem: Explain the difference between reinforcement and punishment in operant conditioning, using an example of each.

steps.text: Operant conditioning concerns how consequences affect the future likelihood of behaviour. Reinforcement increases the behaviour it follows: for example, encouraging feedback contingent on completing a practice task may make completing such tasks more likely. Calling the feedback a reinforcer requires its behavioural effect, rather than assuming every pleasant event necessarily works.

Punishment decreases the behaviour it follows. For example, losing access to a valued game after breaking an agreed rule could reduce future rule-breaking. Positive and negative refer to adding or removing a consequence, not to whether it is morally good or bad. The distinction rests on the direction of behavioural change and the contingency involved.

subject: psychology
title: Organizing knowledge with schemas
stem: Explain schema theory with reference to one example of cognition.

steps.text: Schema theory proposes that organized prior knowledge guides how people interpret and remember information. A restaurant schema, for example, contains expectations about ordering, receiving food and paying. It can help a person understand an unfamiliar restaurant quickly without reconstructing the purpose of every action from the beginning.

The same expectations may also lead the person to infer a typical event that did not occur, such as remembering table service in a self-service venue. This illustrates both efficient interpretation and possible reconstructive error. Schemas are flexible knowledge structures rather than fixed records that determine every perception, and unexpected experience can prompt their revision.

subject: psychology
title: An irrelevant starting estimate
stem: A community centre must estimate the preparation time for a new well-being workshop. Before reviewing the actual tasks, one planner sees a random demonstration number labelled “twelve hours”. The planner keeps using twelve as the starting point despite knowing that the number was unrelated to the workshop. Explain how anchoring bias could affect the estimate and distinguish it from using relevant prior experience.

steps.text: The arbitrary duration can become a reference from which the planner adjusts rather than constructing an estimate from the required tasks. Insufficient adjustment could leave the judgement inappropriately close to twelve hours even after the planner recognizes that the number provides no evidence about the workshop.

Knowing that a reference is irrelevant does not necessarily remove its influence. A stronger estimate would connect preparation activities, available staff and relevant experience to the judgement. The scenario does not establish how many hours are actually needed, so the answer should explain the possible reasoning bias rather than declare a particular numerical estimate correct.

Relevant prior experience differs because a comparable workshop may provide justified information about task demands. It can still be overgeneralized, but its evidential value needs evaluation. Anchoring here is the undue persistence of an arbitrary reference, not the claim that every starting estimate or use of experience is irrational.

subject: psychology
title: A cue in a waiting room
stem: In a fictional account, a distinctive waiting-room chime was initially unremarkable to an adult. Across several visits, the chime preceded an unpleasant procedure that elicited tension. Later, the adult feels tension on hearing the chime even during a visit without that procedure. Apply classical conditioning to this account. Do not propose a procedure for deliberately distressing participants.

steps.text: The unpleasant procedure is the unconditioned stimulus and tension to it is the unconditioned response in this account. The chime begins as a neutral stimulus relative to that response. Repeatedly preceding the procedure can make the chime a predictive cue rather than a biologically necessary cause of tension.

The chime can then function as a conditioned stimulus, with tension in its presence becoming a conditioned response. Its occurrence during a visit without the procedure illustrates responding to a learned predictor when the original eliciting event is absent. The response need not reproduce every feature or intensity of the original tension.

This is an explanation based on a stimulus association, not a claim that tension was rewarded or voluntarily chosen. Other expectations may contribute, so the narrative is compatible with conditioning without proving that conditioning is the only process involved. Responsible discussion should explain the supplied case rather than recommend inducing distress to demonstrate it.

subject: psychology
title: A demanding information leaflet
stem: A well-being centre gives newcomers an unfamiliar activity schedule. Instructions on one page refer repeatedly to symbols on a separate page, so readers must switch between them while remembering several steps. A designer proposes placing each explanation beside its symbol. Apply cognitive load theory to explain why this could help, and why the change need not help every reader equally.

steps.text: The newcomers must understand unfamiliar steps while maintaining links between symbols and explanations. Switching pages adds a coordination demand that does not itself serve the goal of understanding the schedule. Limited working-memory resources can be occupied by searching and retaining these links rather than organizing the activity information.

Integrating each explanation with its symbol could reduce this avoidable demand and make relevant relationships easier to process. The claim concerns presentation and available resources, not a diagnosis of low intelligence or a preference for a fixed visual learning style. The actual content can still require deliberate thought.

Experienced readers may already know the symbols and sequence, so the original presentation imposes less additional demand on them. Excessive explanation could even become redundant. The theory therefore predicts a conditional benefit depending on knowledge and task demands, rather than guaranteeing that one simplified leaflet is best for every person and purpose.

subject: psychology
title: A cognitive cycle of worry
stem: An illustrative cognitive model proposes this cycle: interpreting an ambiguous message as threatening directs attention toward possible dangers; noticing those dangers then strengthens the threatening interpretation. Explain how the model could account for persistent worry and identify one limitation of the explanation. The model is supplied for analysis, not as a clinical assessment of a real individual.

steps.text: The model identifies a feedback relationship rather than treating each thought as independent. A threatening interpretation changes which information receives attention, and the selected information then appears to confirm that interpretation. Worry can persist even though the original message was ambiguous because the person repeatedly processes evidence through the same cycle.

The explanation generates a specific possibility: changing interpretation or the allocation of attention might disrupt the proposed relationship. However, the diagram alone is not evidence that either process causes the other. The model would need relevant observations and comparisons rather than relying on the intuitive appeal of arrows.

One limitation is that persistent worry may also depend on circumstances, bodily states and prior experiences not represented in the simplified cycle. Real danger should not automatically be dismissed as distorted thinking. The model is useful for representing a possible maintenance process, while its completeness and applicability to an individual remain separate questions.

subject: psychology
title: What a teacher records
stem: A teacher initially believes that a child gives up too easily on puzzles. The teacher records occasions when the child stops but rarely records occasions when the child persists or improves. Apply confirmation bias to explain how the teacher could maintain the initial belief. Explain why the account does not establish the child’s actual developmental capacity.

steps.text: The initial belief guides which examples are noticed and retained. Recording stopping behaviour while overlooking persistence creates a selective record that can appear to confirm the belief. The teacher is not simply collecting all relevant observations and then reaching an unfavourable conclusion; the selection itself privileges confirming evidence.

An adequate account identifies the missing comparison: episodes of persistence, the demands of different puzzles and changes over time are relevant to the claim. A child might reasonably stop an unsuitable task, and stopping once does not establish a stable disposition. The biased record conceals these distinctions.

The scenario therefore explains a possible process maintaining the teacher’s judgement, not the child’s true limits. Expectations may also influence opportunities and feedback. Responsibility includes seeking meaningful counterexamples and revising labels when warranted, rather than treating a selective account as evidence that the child cannot develop persistence or benefit from support.

subject: psychology
title: A quick choice and a reconsidered choice
stem: In a fictional school discussion, an adolescent immediately prefers a familiar project design. When asked to consider the project’s unfamiliar constraints, the adolescent deliberately compares alternatives and changes the choice. Apply dual processing theory. Explain why the account does not show that every adolescent’s first choice is wrong.

steps.text: Familiarity can support a relatively automatic response that requires little deliberate comparison. Considering new constraints then recruits more attention-demanding processing, allowing the adolescent to represent additional information and compare possibilities. The changed choice is compatible with a shift in the contribution of these processes.

Dual processing is not a developmental rule that adolescents possess only fast processing or that adults always deliberate. The scenario demonstrates one person’s processing under particular task demands. A familiar design might have been suitable, and deliberate analysis could also misinterpret a constraint or rationalize an initial preference.

The defensible explanation relates familiarity, available attention and the relevance of the new information to the judgement. Whether the revised choice is better requires criteria about the project’s goals. Speed and later revision alone do not establish accuracy, developmental immaturity or a universal need to reject first impressions.

subject: psychology
title: Removing repeated reminders
stem: In a fictional household, a young person dislikes repeated reminders about an agreed voluntary tidying routine. Completing the routine promptly stops the reminders, and prompt completion becomes more frequent. Explain the operant conditioning process illustrated. Distinguish it from punishment without recommending the arrangement as a parenting technique.

steps.text: Prompt completion is followed by removal of an experience the young person finds aversive: repeated reminders. Because prompt completion becomes more frequent, the supplied consequence functions as reinforcement. It is negative reinforcement because something is removed, not because the effect is morally negative.

Punishment would reduce the future likelihood of the behaviour it follows. The scenario instead describes an increase in prompt completion, so labelling it punishment merely because reminders are unpleasant confuses the stimulus’s quality with the direction of behavioural change. The relevant contingency is completion followed by cessation of reminders.

The scenario supplies the behavioural pattern needed to classify the process, but does not show that this is the only reason for change or an appropriate household policy. Agreement, autonomy and unintended effects matter. Explaining a learning contingency is different from endorsing every situation in which the contingency could operate.

subject: psychology
title: Revising a familiar category
stem: A child initially expects all library books to tell invented stories. The child interprets a new wildlife book as a story until discussion and further examples show that some library books provide factual explanations. Apply schema theory to explain both the initial interpretation and the later revision. No particular age or developmental stage is specified.

steps.text: The child’s existing organized knowledge of library books guides interpretation of the unfamiliar example. Expecting an invented story makes that interpretation readily available, so the child initially fits the wildlife book into the established schema rather than independently determining every feature of its purpose.

Discussion and further examples provide information that does not fit the original expectation. The child can revise the schema to include different purposes, distinguishing factual explanation from invented narrative. This shows that a schema can organize experience while remaining responsive to inconsistent information.

The explanation does not require a fixed developmental stage or imply that the child is incapable of learning until a particular birthday. Nor does it establish a universal sequence for all children. It connects prior knowledge, interpretation and revision to the specific example, while recognizing that educational experience affects which expectations are available.

subject: psychology
title: A starting point in a shared decision
stem: Two adults are negotiating how to divide the time required for a shared voluntary project. Before listing the tasks, one casually proposes that the other do most of the work. Later revisions remain close to that initial proposal, although neither person has justified it. Apply anchoring bias and explain why disagreement alone would not establish this bias.

steps.text: The initial proposal can become the reference around which later negotiation occurs. If revisions remain insufficiently adjusted to the actual tasks and available time, the starting allocation may exert more influence than its evidential basis warrants. A social proposal can therefore serve as an anchor without being a random number.

The relevant question is whether judgement is unduly tied to that starting point. The adults may have legitimate reasons for an unequal division, such as differing skills or availability. Those reasons would need examination before concluding that unequal work or disagreement necessarily reflects a cognitive bias.

Anchoring provides one possible explanation of the persistence of an unjustified allocation, not a judgement about either adult’s motives. Responsibility in applying the concept includes distinguishing unfairness, deliberate bargaining and biased estimation. A reasoned explanation relates the initial reference to later adjustment rather than labelling every difficult negotiation irrational.

subject: psychology
title: A family-call cue and an automatic response
stem: In a fictional account, a previously unremarkable family-video-call tone repeatedly precedes a brief, unexpected burst of loud microphone feedback. The feedback elicits an automatic startle response. Later, the tone alone elicits anticipatory tension before any feedback occurs. Apply classical conditioning and distinguish this account from an operant explanation of choosing to mute the call. Do not propose a procedure for deliberately distressing participants.

steps.text: The sudden loud feedback is the unconditioned stimulus and its automatic startle effect is the unconditioned response. The family-call tone begins as neutral relative to this response. By repeatedly preceding the feedback, the tone can become a conditioned stimulus that elicits anticipatory tension even when no feedback follows. A conditioned response need not duplicate every feature of the original startle.

An operant explanation would instead examine the consequences of muting behaviour. If muting removes an aversive sound and becomes more frequent, that would illustrate negative reinforcement. This concerns a chosen action and its consequences, whereas the classical account concerns an elicited response to a predictive cue. Both processes could operate without being interchangeable explanations.

The family-call context may consequently acquire an unwelcome emotional meaning even though the tone itself did not initially elicit tension. The supplied narrative supports applying the model, not proving that every reaction during a family interaction is conditioned. Explaining it does not require or justify deliberately exposing participants to distressing noise.

subject: psychology
title: Several demands during a conversation
stem: During a difficult planning conversation, an adult also monitors several message threads and remembers instructions for an unfamiliar booking system. The adult misses part of the partner’s explanation. Apply cognitive load theory to this situation and explain why the missed explanation does not by itself show a lack of care.

steps.text: The person is maintaining and coordinating several kinds of information while attempting to understand the conversation. An unfamiliar booking system can demand conscious processing that an experienced user might perform more easily. Together with monitoring messages, this can leave insufficient working-memory resources for integrating the partner’s explanation.

The theory explains a possible limit on processing at that moment, rather than measuring the person’s affection or stable intelligence. Missing information is compatible with overload, although deliberate inattention or other factors remain possible. The observation alone does not uniquely identify any one explanation.

Reducing competing demands or externalizing booking instructions could make the conversation easier to follow, but effectiveness depends on the actual bottleneck. A responsible application avoids using limited capacity as an automatic excuse for every misunderstanding. It relates the concurrent demands to processing and distinguishes this mechanism from conclusions about the relationship’s quality.

subject: psychology
title: Where a remembered request can fail
stem: A supplied cognitive model distinguishes encoding a request, maintaining it while occupied and retrieving it later. An adult hears a partner’s request while distracted and later forgets it. Explain how the model helps generate alternative explanations, and why forgetting alone cannot reveal which process failed.

steps.text: The model separates possible processing problems that can produce a similar final outcome. Distraction may prevent effective encoding, so the request is never represented well enough for later use. Alternatively, it may be encoded but poorly maintained while other demands compete, or available information may not be retrieved at the required time.

These alternatives matter because simply calling the person forgetful does not identify the process. Appropriate additional information about attention, immediate recall or useful retrieval cues could help discriminate possibilities. The model generates questions and predictions rather than directly observing the contents of an invisible memory store.

A forgotten request therefore does not prove a lack of concern or identify one particular memory component. Nor do the model’s labels establish separate anatomical locations. Its value is a clearer set of explanations that can be evaluated against relevant evidence, while recognizing that motivation, communication and relationship context may also influence what happens.

subject: psychology
title: A rule that is never challenged
stem: Students propose that every object sorted into a fictional “Luma” category must have a stripe. When allowed to ask about new examples, they choose only striped objects that they already expect to be Luma and overlook opportunities to ask about unstriped examples. Explain how confirmation bias could limit their learning of the category rule.

steps.text: The students seek examples likely to fit their preferred explanation rather than testing information that could reveal its inadequacy. If some unstriped objects can also be Luma, examining only apparently confirming examples may leave the overly restrictive rule unchallenged. A sequence of positive cases does not establish that no counterexample exists.

The relevant issue is the diagnostic value of the chosen examples, not a requirement that every question must produce a negative answer. Comparing competing rules can make a carefully selected confirming case informative. Here, however, the students neglect available cases that would distinguish their stripe rule from broader alternatives.

The scenario does not disclose the actual rule, so an answer should not invent it. It explains why the selection strategy can preserve an inadequate hypothesis and restrict learning. Actively considering what would count against a proposed rule is different from simply becoming more confident after collecting examples consistent with it.

title: A familiar answer in a new task
stem: A learner instantly chooses a familiar procedure for a new task. A prompt then draws attention to a changed constraint, and the learner deliberately checks whether the procedure still applies. Use dual processing theory to explain why the check could improve learning, and why deliberate checking is not guaranteed to produce a correct answer.

steps.text: The familiar procedure can be triggered relatively automatically, reducing the effort needed to begin. That efficiency is useful when the new task genuinely matches prior experience. A changed constraint may make the familiar response unsuitable, so deliberate checking allows the learner to represent the difference and evaluate the procedure’s applicability.

The benefit comes from considering relevant information, not from slowness itself. Deliberate processing also depends on knowledge and can be directed toward defending an initial response. A learner who misunderstands the changed constraint might spend more time and still choose an inappropriate procedure.

The theory therefore supports a conditional role for checking when automatic transfer may be misleading. It does not require replacing all fluent expertise with exhaustive deliberation. Explaining how the task differs and how the check uses that distinction connects the processing account to learning more precisely than assuming every first answer must be rejected.

subject: psychology
title: A consequence that changes participation
stem: In a fictional learning club, a student earns a token immediately after submitting a short practice explanation. Tokens can be exchanged for a chosen optional club activity. Submitting explanations becomes more frequent. Explain the operant process illustrated and why the tokens’ pleasantness alone would not have been enough to classify it.

steps.text: The supplied contingency adds a token after the target behaviour, and the behaviour becomes more frequent. The consequence therefore functions as positive reinforcement in this account. Positive refers to adding something, while reinforcement refers to the increase in future submission of explanations.

A token does not automatically reinforce every student or behaviour simply because the club intends it as a reward. Its function is identified by its effect in the relevant contingency. If submissions did not increase, calling it reinforcement solely because it appeared attractive would confuse an intended reward with a demonstrated behavioural function.

The scenario supports the classification but not the claim that token use improves deep understanding, intrinsic interest or long-term learning. Those are different outcomes. An accurate explanation distinguishes increased submission from educational quality and avoids assuming that an immediate change in participation establishes the best approach to teaching.

subject: psychology
title: Remembering an unfamiliar exhibition
stem: A learner visits an exhibition arranged unlike a conventional museum. Later, the learner remembers a ticket desk near the entrance, although the exhibition had no ticket desk. The learner often visits ticketed museums. Apply schema theory to explain a possible source of the remembered detail, and identify a limit of that explanation.

steps.text: Prior museum experiences can produce an organized expectation about entrances, tickets and display areas. This schema helps interpret the new exhibition, but may also contribute a typical detail when the visit is reconstructed later. The remembered desk could be an inference consistent with prior knowledge rather than a preserved record of the particular event.

The explanation does not imply deliberate dishonesty or that all remembered details are inaccurate. Schemas usually support efficient understanding, and the error concerns a specific plausible addition. Describing the expectation and its possible contribution is more precise than merely stating that memory is unreliable.

The scenario alone does not establish that a schema caused the error. Confusion with another visit, suggestions from another person or ambiguity in the question are possible alternatives. The account is a plausible interpretation that would require appropriate evidence to distinguish it from these explanations, rather than a direct observation of a schema inside the learner’s mind.

subject: psychology
title: Confirmation and the evaluation of well-being claims
stem: Discuss how confirmation bias can affect the responsible evaluation of claims about psychological well-being. In your response, consider the concepts of bias, responsibility and causality.

steps.text: A claim about psychological well-being may attract support because it fits an existing belief about what makes people feel better. Confirmation bias can influence which accounts are sought, how ambiguous experiences are interpreted and which failures are remembered. A person might collect enthusiastic testimonials for a favoured programme while discounting reports that it did not help.

The causal problem is that apparent improvement can have several explanations. Expectations, changing circumstances or other support may contribute, and selective attention to successes can conceal these possibilities. Responsible evaluation therefore asks whether the evidence distinguishes the proposed explanation from alternatives, rather than treating agreement with a prior belief as a sufficient test.

Bias can also operate against an unfamiliar claim. Someone committed to an established account may examine a new approach only for weaknesses while excusing comparable weaknesses in familiar approaches. Responsibility requires applying relevant standards consistently, not assuming that scepticism is unbiased simply because it produces a negative judgement.

A counterargument is that prior knowledge legitimately guides evaluation: not every proposal deserves equal confidence or unlimited investigation. This is important because abandoning all expectations would be impractical. The distinction is between revisable expectations supported by relevant knowledge and a process that systematically protects a belief from evidence that could count against it.

Confirmation bias therefore presents a significant risk without explaining every disagreement about well-being. A justified conclusion evaluates how evidence was selected, what would change the evaluator’s mind and whether outcomes actually match the claim. Recognizing bias should improve the standards used to assess a claim, rather than become a label used to dismiss whoever disagrees.

subject: psychology
title: Is deliberation always better for health judgement?
stem: Evaluate the claim that deliberate processing always improves judgements about psychological health and well-being. In your response, consider the concepts of perspective and responsibility.

steps.text: Deliberate processing can improve a judgement when it enables a person to consider relevant alternatives, compare evidence and question an attractive initial impression. For example, a well-being campaign may appear persuasive because its language is familiar. Taking time to inspect what its claims actually mean can reveal unsupported assumptions or outcomes different from those a reader values.

However, the dual processing distinction does not identify accuracy by processing speed. An experienced person may recognize an important pattern efficiently, while extended deliberation can be based on mistaken knowledge. Time spent rehearsing a preferred explanation may strengthen rationalization rather than broaden the range of evidence considered.

The value of deliberation also depends on the decision and available resources. Some judgements allow careful comparison, whereas urgent situations or fatigue constrain it. Requiring exhaustive analysis of every minor choice could itself be burdensome. Responsibility involves deciding when additional checking is likely to provide useful information and when appropriate expert support is needed.

A defence of the claim is that deliberate processing allows errors to be detected that automatic processing may overlook. This is a genuine advantage, but an opportunity is not a guarantee. The process must have access to relevant information, a suitable standard of judgement and enough willingness to revise the first response. Otherwise scrutiny can remain superficial.

The word “always” is therefore unjustified. Deliberation is most useful when a judgement requires comparison that an automatic response does not adequately represent. A stronger conclusion combines efficient processing with targeted review of uncertainty, stakes and evidence. It avoids presenting automatic thought as inherently defective or deliberate thought as a universally reliable route to well-being.

subject: psychology
title: Rewarding a health-related habit
stem: Examine the value and limitations of operant conditioning for explaining sustained changes in voluntary health-related habits. In your response, consider the concepts of change, responsibility and causality.

steps.text: Operant conditioning can explain how consequences alter the likelihood of a habit. An adult who chooses a regular activity may become more likely to repeat it when the activity is followed by a valued social experience or encouraging feedback. The explanatory claim concerns the relationship between behaviour and its consequences, not merely whether someone describes an incentive as pleasant.

This perspective makes useful distinctions between beginning a behaviour, repeating it under a particular contingency and sustaining it after that contingency changes. Increased participation while an external reward is available does not establish persistence after its removal. Understanding the conditions under which the behaviour continues is necessary before claiming a lasting health-related change.

The account also has limits as a complete explanation. Access, personal goals, fatigue and the meaning of the activity affect whether a consequence is available or valued. More frequent performance is not automatically healthier, and a measure of participation should not be substituted for psychological well-being or physical benefit without justification.

A counterargument is that goals and preferences themselves can be shaped by learning history, so an operant explanation can incorporate more than simple prizes. This strengthens its explanatory range, but does not remove the need to specify observable contingencies and distinguish the account from explanations that would predict the same outcome. Broad flexibility must not become an unfalsifiable claim that every change was reinforced.

Operant conditioning is therefore valuable for analysing particular patterns of habit change but insufficient to guarantee sustained beneficial outcomes. Responsible application respects voluntary choice, avoids coercive contingencies and evaluates maintenance alongside relevant outcomes. The best conclusion links specific consequences to a defined behaviour while acknowledging the wider circumstances that enable or constrain change.

subject: psychology
title: Schemas and the meaning of a symptom report
stem: Discuss how schema theory can inform the interpretation of people’s reports of psychological well-being without dismissing their experiences as unreal. In your response, consider the concepts of measurement, perspective and responsibility.

steps.text: Schema theory proposes that prior knowledge organizes attention, interpretation and recall. Expectations about stress or well-being may influence which experiences a person notices and how those experiences are described. For example, someone expecting a difficult transition may interpret a temporary lapse in concentration differently from someone who sees the transition as an opportunity.

This perspective matters for measurement because a report is not a transparent recording of an experience independent of language and prior understanding. Question wording and available categories can interact with schemas. Two people with similar experiences may use different labels, while the same person may describe an earlier experience differently after acquiring a new explanatory framework.

However, interpretation is not equivalent to fabrication. An experience can be distressing and consequential even when its meaning is shaped by expectations. It would be irresponsible to use schema theory as an automatic reason to dismiss reports or assume that correcting a belief will remove every difficulty. Biological conditions and present circumstances may also contribute.

One counterargument is that emphasizing schemas makes reports seem too subjective to be useful. This conclusion is too strong: structured questions, contextual information and converging indicators can improve interpretation. The purpose is to clarify what a measure captures and why reports may differ, rather than replace the person’s account with a supposedly assumption-free judgement.

Schema theory consequently provides a useful partial explanation of how well-being is understood and communicated. A balanced conclusion distinguishes the reality of an experience from the processes used to categorize and recall it. Responsible measurement listens to reports, examines context and treats alternative interpretations as questions to investigate rather than as proof that the experience never occurred.

subject: psychology
title: An early label as a reference point
stem: Evaluate the role of anchoring bias in adults’ judgements of a developing child’s abilities. In your response, consider the concepts of bias, measurement and change.

steps.text: Adults often make judgements about developing abilities from incomplete information. An early label or initial performance can become a reference point against which later behaviour is interpreted. If adjustment is insufficient, a child who struggled on an unfamiliar first task may continue to be judged as generally incapable despite later progress or evidence from different tasks.

Anchoring is useful here because it identifies a particular judgement process: undue influence of the initial reference. It is not synonymous with every expectation or all prejudice. An earlier observation may contain relevant information, but its weight should depend on task conditions, subsequent evidence and the developmental change being assessed rather than on its position at the beginning.

Measurement complicates the inference. A difficult first task could reflect language familiarity, instructions, fatigue or limited opportunity rather than the broad ability adults intend to judge. Later assessments may also measure different skills. Claims about insufficient adjustment require a clear account of what has changed and what evidence should reasonably alter the judgement.

A counterargument is that apparent persistence of an initial judgement may reflect stable performance or relevant experience rather than an anchor. This matters because disagreement with an optimistic later interpretation does not itself demonstrate bias. Competing explanations should be considered, including whether adults had access to the same evidence and whether their criteria were appropriate.

Anchoring can therefore help explain some persistent labels but cannot be assumed from a single developmental judgement. A defensible conclusion encourages revisable assessments and attention to new evidence, while distinguishing arbitrary references from justified knowledge. The concept is strongest when it explains how a starting point distorts interpretation, rather than simply criticizing any continuity in adults’ expectations.

subject: psychology
title: Learned emotional responses across development
stem: To what extent can classical conditioning explain changes in emotional responses during human development? In your response, consider the concepts of change and causality.

steps.text: Classical conditioning can explain how a previously neutral cue acquires emotional significance through its relationship with another event. A child may come to anticipate enjoyment at a location repeatedly associated with welcoming activities, or discomfort at a cue associated with an unpleasant experience. The explanation connects changing responses to learning history rather than assuming the response was present from birth.

This account can also explain why responses change when predictive relationships change. Repeated safe experiences with a cue may reduce a conditioned response. However, reduced responding does not necessarily mean the original association has been erased: the context and later experiences may affect whether a response returns. Development should not be represented as a simple permanent deletion of earlier learning.

Causal interpretation nevertheless requires care. Emotional development involves interpretation, observation of others, maturation and changing social conditions. A cue may be meaningful because a child has been told what it signifies, rather than because the child directly experienced repeated pairings. Similar outward responses can therefore arise through different pathways.

A defence of conditioning is that these additional processes can interact with learned associations rather than refute them. This is reasonable, but the account still needs predictions that identify the contribution of a particular association. If every emotional change is retrospectively described as conditioning without specifying relevant stimuli or learning history, the explanation loses precision.

Classical conditioning consequently explains important components of developmental emotional change, especially when a cue’s predictive history is clear. Its reach is partial rather than universal. A stronger conclusion integrates associations with cognitive and social processes, acknowledges context-sensitive change and avoids treating learned responses as either inevitable or permanently fixed after a single experience.

subject: psychology
title: Instruction for developing learners
stem: Discuss the value and limitations of cognitive load theory when designing instruction for developing learners. In your response, consider the concepts of perspective, responsibility and change.

steps.text: Cognitive load theory offers a useful perspective on the demands instruction places on limited working-memory resources. A novice who must interpret unfamiliar symbols, remember several steps and search separate explanations may have little capacity left to organize the underlying relationships. Reducing avoidable searching can make the same content more accessible without changing its educational purpose.

Development matters, but chronological age is not the only relevant difference. Prior knowledge can organize information into meaningful units, making a complex task less demanding for an experienced learner. Instruction suitable for one learner may therefore be unnecessarily detailed or insufficiently supported for another learner of a similar age.

Responsibility requires distinguishing supportive design from a fixed judgement of capacity. A learner’s difficulty with one presentation does not prove low intelligence or a permanent limit. Language, accessibility and opportunity also affect demands. The theory should guide revisable decisions about tasks and support rather than justify excluding learners from challenging material.

A counterargument is that reducing demands too far may remove the activity needed to build understanding. This is important: effortless performance during instruction is not identical to lasting learning. Useful design can reduce irrelevant demands while retaining appropriately supported reasoning, and the balance may change as knowledge develops. One universal rule that all difficulty is harmful is not supported.

subject: psychology
title: What a developmental cognitive model explains
stem: Examine the value and limitations of cognitive models for explaining developmental change. Refer to at least one model or clearly specified example. In your response, consider the concepts of perspective, measurement and change.

steps.text: A cognitive model can clarify what is proposed to change as learners develop, instead of using age itself as an explanation. For example, a model may distinguish changes in maintaining information, directing attention and organizing prior knowledge. It can generate different predictions about why a learner succeeds on one task but struggles when several demands must be coordinated.

The value of this approach is explanatory precision. If a child’s improvement is attributed to a particular process, researchers can ask what other tasks should improve and under which conditions. Models also make assumptions visible, allowing alternatives such as continuous improvement and more qualitative reorganization to be compared rather than treated as interchangeable descriptions.

Measurement presents a challenge because task performance can depend on understanding instructions, language and motivation as well as the target process. A model that interprets every failure as absence of an ability may underestimate what a learner can do in a more suitable task. Developmental inferences need to distinguish change in the proposed process from changes in other demands.

A counterargument is that simplification is unavoidable and does not invalidate a model. This is correct: no model can reproduce every feature of development. The relevant test is whether its simplifications support useful, discriminating predictions and acknowledge circumstances where they fail. Adding a new unmeasured component for every unexpected result would weaken rather than improve explanatory value.

Cognitive models consequently provide important tools for understanding developmental change, but their components should remain testable constructs rather than literal containers or universal age labels. A justified conclusion assesses the particular process, evidence and competing explanation. Models are most useful when they explain patterns of change and guide better questions, rather than merely rename an age-related performance difference.

subject: psychology
title: Confirmation during interpersonal disagreement
stem: Evaluate the claim that confirmation bias is the main cause of persistent interpersonal disagreement. In your response, consider the concepts of bias, perspective and responsibility.

steps.text: Confirmation bias can contribute to persistent disagreement when people selectively notice or interpret evidence supporting an existing view of each other. Someone who expects a partner to be inconsiderate may remember delayed replies while overlooking reliable support. Each new ambiguity can then appear to confirm the established interpretation, making revision less likely.

This mechanism explains persistence more precisely than simply saying that people refuse to agree. It identifies how the available information is treated and suggests that genuinely diagnostic counterexamples may be ignored. The same process can affect both positive and negative expectations; maintaining an unrealistically favourable view can also involve selective interpretation.

However, disagreement may reflect different values, interests, access to information or actual harmful behaviour. These are not automatically cognitive errors. A person may reasonably maintain a judgement because the counterexamples are weak or irrelevant. Treating every justified concern as confirmation bias risks shifting responsibility away from behaviour that needs to be addressed.

A defence of the claim is that even real differences are interpreted through prior expectations, so bias can amplify nearly any conflict. This supports its possible contribution, but does not establish that it is the main cause. Demonstrating primacy requires comparison with other explanations and a clear definition of whether the outcome is disagreement, hostility or failure to resolve a practical problem.

The general claim is therefore too strong. Confirmation bias is a plausible maintenance process in some interpersonal disagreements, but its role depends on the evidence and context. A responsible conclusion examines selective reasoning without using a bias label to dismiss legitimate perspectives, and distinguishes improving the evaluation of evidence from requiring everyone to reach the same judgement.

subject: psychology
title: Deliberation during disagreement
stem: Discuss whether deliberate processing is more useful than automatic processing for resolving interpersonal disagreements. In your response, consider the concepts of perspective and change.

steps.text: Deliberate processing can help when an immediate interpretation overlooks another person’s perspective or a relevant constraint. Pausing to distinguish what was said from what was inferred may make alternative explanations available. In a disagreement about a missed commitment, deliberate consideration of circumstances can prevent a familiar negative interpretation from being accepted without inspection.

Automatic processing nevertheless has useful functions. Familiar social skills can enable fluent listening and recognition of emotional cues without consciously rehearsing every step. An experienced person may respond sensitively through well-practised processes. Requiring constant explicit analysis could disrupt an interaction or consume resources needed to attend to the other person.

Nor is deliberate thought necessarily fair. People can use effort to construct arguments defending their own position, repeatedly revisit grievances or interpret ambiguous evidence through an existing belief. More thinking improves resolution only if it is directed toward relevant information and revisable understanding, rather than toward more elaborate rationalization.

A counterargument is that automatic social reactions often reproduce prejudice or habitual hostility, so deliberate checking remains essential. This is persuasive in situations where a habitual response is poorly suited to the evidence or the stakes. It supports targeted review, however, rather than a universal ranking of processing types independent of the task, knowledge and emotional conditions.

Neither type is therefore uniformly more useful. Effective resolution may combine fluent interpersonal skills with deliberate examination of uncertain interpretations and consequences. A qualified judgement defines what resolution means, considers whether the disagreement involves a cognitive misunderstanding or a substantive conflict, and evaluates whether the chosen process actually helps rather than assuming that slower thought is automatically wiser.

subject: psychology
title: Consequences, cooperation and autonomy
stem: Examine the value and ethical limitations of explaining cooperation in human relationships through operant conditioning. In your response, consider the concepts of causality, responsibility and change.

steps.text: Operant conditioning can explain how responses from others influence future cooperative behaviour. Appreciation following a helpful action may make similar actions more likely, while an aversive consequence may reduce a particular response. The account directs attention to actual contingencies rather than assuming that an intended reward necessarily has its intended effect.

Its value is especially clear when patterns of consequences unintentionally maintain a behaviour. For example, an apparently discouraging reaction may still provide attention that the person values. However, this remains a hypothesis about a specified behavioural pattern, not a reason to assume that every social response is motivated by obtaining rewards.

Cooperation also involves goals, norms, interpretation and mutual commitments. The same response can be understood as appreciation, manipulation or an obligation depending on the relationship. A behavioural description may predict repetition without fully explaining what the action means to the people involved or whether the relationship is fair.

A defence of the operant perspective is that acknowledging these meanings does not remove the influence of consequences. This is reasonable, but explanatory relevance does not justify any intervention designed to control another person. Autonomy, consent, dependence and the possibility of coercion matter, especially when one person controls access to valued resources or social contact.

Operant conditioning is therefore useful as one analysis of how cooperation changes, while limited as a complete account or ethical justification. Responsible use distinguishes understanding a contingency from endorsing manipulation, and evaluates consequences for both parties. A stronger conclusion integrates behavioural effects with the purposes and responsibilities of the relationship rather than reducing cooperation to compliance obtained by incentives.

subject: psychology
title: Relationship expectations and their revision
stem: Discuss how schemas can both support and obstruct the development of human relationships. In your response, consider the concepts of perspective, change and bias.

steps.text: Schemas organize prior social knowledge and expectations, allowing people to interpret familiar interactions efficiently. Expectations about friendship, for example, can help someone anticipate reciprocity, understand an invitation and coordinate shared activities. Without organized prior knowledge, each social event would require extensive interpretation from the beginning.

The same organization can obstruct a developing relationship when expectations are applied too rigidly. A person may interpret an unfamiliar communication style as disinterest because it does not match a familiar pattern. Recalling schema-consistent episodes more readily can maintain this interpretation even when other interactions suggest a different meaning.

Change is therefore central. New experiences may refine a schema or reveal that different people and situations require different expectations. However, a single contradictory event does not always require abandoning well-supported prior knowledge. The question is whether the schema is being appropriately updated or protected from evidence that should meaningfully challenge it.

A counterargument is that focusing on schemas underestimates differences in actual behaviour and unequal power. Some expectations may be accurate, and harmful treatment should not be reframed automatically as a misunderstanding produced by the recipient’s knowledge structures. A schema explanation needs to distinguish the person’s interpretation from the events and social conditions being interpreted.

Schemas consequently support relationships through efficient understanding while risking bias and rigidity. Their effect depends on fit, flexibility and the quality of new information. A balanced conclusion neither treats expectations as inherently harmful nor presents them as fixed scripts; it examines how people use and revise prior knowledge while acknowledging the reality and responsibilities of their interactions.

subject: psychology
title: Reference examples and grading judgements
stem: Examine how anchoring bias can affect judgements of learners’ work, while distinguishing an inappropriate anchor from a legitimate assessment standard. In your response, consider the concepts of bias, measurement and responsibility.

steps.text: A teacher judging unfamiliar work may be influenced by an initial score, a previous learner’s response or an early impression. If later judgement remains unduly close to that reference despite relevant evidence, anchoring can distort the assessment. The concern is not merely variation between scores but an influence unsupported by the criteria used to judge the work.

A legitimate standard serves a different role. A clearly justified example can illustrate what a criterion requires and help assessors interpret it consistently. Its influence is appropriate insofar as the judgement remains tied to the actual features of the learner’s response. The same numerical reference can therefore be useful or misleading depending on its basis and use.

Measurement requires separating target achievement from irrelevant information such as a learner’s earlier reputation. An assessor who begins from a prior score may fail to recognize improvement or a different demand in the present task. In contrast, changing a score merely to move away from the reference would not improve validity if the original score was warranted.

One counterargument is that experienced assessors cannot judge without reference to prior examples. This is correct and shows why eliminating all references is neither possible nor desirable. The stronger aim is to examine whether relevant criteria and evidence govern adjustment, including occasions when the new work meaningfully differs from the reference example.

Anchoring thus presents a plausible threat to fair measurement, but cannot be inferred solely because assessors use standards or produce similar scores. Responsible judgement makes the basis of comparison explicit, tests early impressions against the full response and remains open to justified revision. The concept is most useful when it identifies undue persistence of a reference rather than condemning comparison itself.

subject: psychology
title: Classroom emotion is not the whole of learning
stem: Evaluate the claim that classical conditioning provides a sufficient explanation of emotional responses to learning environments. In your response, consider the concepts of causality, change and perspective.

steps.text: Classical conditioning can explain how a learning environment acquires emotional significance through association. A previously unremarkable room or sound might come to predict supportive activities or unpleasant experiences. Responding to that cue before the next event occurs is consistent with learning a predictive relationship between stimuli.

This explanation has value because emotional responses need not reflect the immediate event alone. An apparently safe task can evoke tension through its connection with earlier experiences. Similarly, familiar contextual cues can support anticipation of enjoyable learning. The account identifies a possible history linking a present response to a cue.

However, students can also respond to meanings acquired through discussion, observation, goals or current treatment. A learner may feel concern because an assessment has real consequences, without needing repeated direct pairings of a neutral cue and an unpleasant event. Different processes can produce similar outward behaviour, so the response itself does not uniquely identify conditioning.

A defence of the claim is that conditioning may contribute alongside these processes and that cognitive expectations can interact with associations. This supports an integrated explanation but undermines sufficiency: if additional processes are required to explain how a cue is interpreted and why its relevance changes, conditioning alone does not provide the entire account. An explanation should state what its own mechanism specifically predicts.

The sufficiency claim is therefore too strong. Classical conditioning offers a useful explanation for some cue-related emotional changes but not every response to a learning environment. A balanced conclusion considers direct experience, interpretation and social conditions, while recognizing that supportive change should not be reduced to deliberately exposing learners to distressing demonstrations of conditioning.

subject: psychology
title: Should all learning feel easy?
stem: Evaluate the claim that reducing cognitive load as far as possible always improves learning. In your response, consider the concepts of perspective, causality and measurement.

steps.text: Reducing unnecessary cognitive demands can improve learning when limited working-memory resources are diverted from understanding. For example, searching between separated instructions and symbols can require effort that does not help a novice grasp their relationship. Integrating relevant information can free resources for processing the content that matters.

The claim becomes problematic when every form of effort is treated as harmful. Constructing an explanation or applying knowledge to a new situation may be demanding because it requires the very processing that supports learning. Removing that activity can make immediate performance easier while reducing opportunities to develop understanding or transfer.

Prior knowledge also changes what imposes a demand. Detailed support that helps a novice may be redundant for an experienced learner, while unsupported problem solving may overwhelm someone unfamiliar with the content. Consequently, neither maximum guidance nor minimum guidance is universally appropriate, and the relevant comparison depends on the task and learner.

A defence of load reduction is that complex thinking cannot succeed when available resources are already overwhelmed. This is persuasive, but it supports managing demands rather than minimizing all processing. Appropriate sequencing or external support can preserve meaningful reasoning while reducing irrelevant coordination. Claims about improvement also need an outcome: quick completion, delayed retention and new-task transfer are not interchangeable.

The word “always” is therefore unwarranted. Cognitive load theory is useful for identifying avoidable demands and matching support to knowledge, but ease is not a complete measure of learning. A justified conclusion evaluates which demands are reduced, which learning processes remain and whether the resulting gains extend beyond a smoothly completed practice task.

subject: psychology
title: How to judge a memory model
stem: Discuss how psychologists can judge the usefulness of a cognitive model of memory. Refer to at least one model or clearly specified example. In your response, consider the concepts of measurement, perspective and causality.

steps.text: A useful cognitive model of memory should do more than rename successful and unsuccessful remembering. It should specify proposed processes and generate predictions that can be compared with performance. For example, distinguishing verbal and visuospatial maintenance can predict why certain pairs of concurrent tasks interfere more than others under particular conditions.

Explanatory precision allows comparison with alternatives. If another model explains the same pattern, researchers need observations that distinguish their predictions rather than treating any successful recall as support for every memory theory. A model can be useful for one task while requiring modification or additional processes to explain another.

Measurement is important because memory tasks also require attention, perception, language and strategies. Poor recall does not uniquely identify failure of one proposed component. Converging tasks can strengthen an interpretation, but their demands need examination; a diagram of separate boxes is not itself proof of separate stores or separate anatomical locations.

A counterargument is that a simplified model can remain valuable despite imperfect predictions. This is correct: an accessible representation may guide instruction or help organize research. However, practical convenience should be distinguished from evidence that its mechanisms are accurate. Repeatedly adding unspecified processes after each unexpected outcome can protect a model at the expense of testability.

Usefulness is therefore judged through the clarity and range of predictions, quality of evidence, comparison with alternatives and appropriate applications. A balanced conclusion accepts simplification while requiring explicit limits. The strongest memory model is not necessarily the most detailed diagram, but one that explains relevant patterns and generates informative questions without turning its representational components into unexamined facts.
